sections.title: Literary Ethnography from the East: A Qualitative Writing Workshop
sections.description:
Although little known in the West, there exists a rich history of ethnographic research and writing which emerged in nineteenth and twentieth century Eastern Europe. From Lev Tolstoy’s Caucasian cycle and Anton Chekhov’s Sakhalin Island to Waldemar Bogoras’s “Chuckchee Tales” and sections of Pyotr Kropotkin’s Mutual Aid, the eastern ethnographic tradition has always been intricately intertwined with literature, folklore, and politics.
In this graduate seminar, we explore ethnography as a creative practice through a close reading of primary texts and the critical analysis of secondary sources on the unique trajectories of this understudied East European ethnographic tradition. This seminar will also be offered as a writing collective for graduate students aspiring to write dissertations or articles using ethnographic data. The course will be of interest to graduate students in anthropology, sociology, or any other discipline who wish to read and experiment with literary ethnographic styles of writing.
To think about ethnography as a form of writing, a method of witnessing, and as storytelling, students will collectively work through a series of exercises and mini workshops. The course will explore strategies for describing characters, scenes, subjectivity, and the relationship between theory and narrative. The course will also interrogate the relationship between writing, fieldwork, and fieldnotes, and consider the ethics of ethnographic writing in an academic context. Over the course of the semester, students will work on an ethnographic chapter of their own dissertations or an ethnographic article in preparation for journal submission.
